_fixture: Synthetic example for UI development; not real data. Six 30-minute points from one evening peak.

algorithm.description: Imbalance price split into trend, daily seasonal and remainder by STL and by classical decomposition, with trend and seasonal strengths and three centred smoothers (9-period median, 13-period Savitzky-Golay, 49-period LOWESS).

tables.sample: The gap-free stretch decomposed: its first and last period, its length and how many periods of the range were left out
tables.seasonal_indices: Seasonal effect per phase in GBP/MWh by each method (STL's averaged over cycles), with the first period of each phase
tables.strength: Trend and seasonal strengths from 0 to 1 of the classical decomposition
tables.methods: Whether each decomposition ran; a row that did not explains why

param_descriptions.period: Seasonal period in half-hours (48 = daily, 336 = weekly)
param_descriptions.seasonal_window: STL seasonal smoothing span in cycles; odd, at least 5. STL needs this many complete cycles
param_descriptions.trend_window: STL trend smoothing span in periods; odd, at least 5. null takes Cleveland's default (93 at period 48)
param_descriptions.max_periods: Most recent gap-free periods decomposed (2688 = 56 days)

algorithm.limitations: Retrospective and two-sided: every component and smoother uses later prices as well as earlier ones, so none was knowable at the time and none is a forecast or a feature. Phases count elapsed half-hours from the first decomposed period, so after a clock change the daily profile is an hour off the local clock. The classical trend and remainder are empty within half a period of the stretch's ends, and each smoother within half its window of any gap. Orchid's STL omits the low-pass filter, and a price spike tens of standard deviations high can leak into the seasonal. Strengths describe this stretch only.
